description: The operator's own staff who use the platform every day: the 24/7 support agents who answer WhatsApp, e-mail and chat from the Netherlands, the United States, Sri Lanka and India and reply to every negative Trustpilot review within 48 hours; the growth marketers who buy and re-acquire customers in ten languages and seven currencies with about 80% of demand in the United States and a steep Q4 Year in Review peak; and the production and fulfilment operations managers who run the partner printing facilities on four continents that produce most orders in the customer's country and ship to 150+ countries. In a company modeled at about 75 people, their tooling, the support desk, the growth and campaign console and the production control tower, decides whether a business with no presses of its own and a USD 19.99 entry price keeps its margin, its ratings and its Christmas promises.

customers.name: Customer Support Agent
customers.description: Works one of the 24/7 shifts that PastBook staffs from the Netherlands, the United States, Sri Lanka and India, answering customers on WhatsApp, e-mail and chat in whichever of the ten site languages the ticket arrives in. A typical shift mixes where-is-my-order questions against the published delivery windows (United States 4–8 business days, United Kingdom 4–5, France, the Netherlands, Italy and Germany 3–5, Canada and Australia 5–10), address fixes and cover upgrades that must land before production starts on payment, complaints about colour, binding or a blurry photo the curation engine let through, and the decision whether to reprint from the stored print file or refund. The agent also owns PastBook's public promise on Trustpilot, where the company replies to every negative review, typically within 48 hours, and defends a TrustScore of 4.5 from 35,837 reviews with 79% five-star and 2% one-star. Volume is heavily seasonal: the Q4 Year in Review and gift peak multiplies contacts, and a Christmas cut-off missed in one time zone becomes a refund in another.

Authority and a one-click path to reprint from the stored print file or refund within a set limit without escalating to a manager in another time zone
Delivery windows, Christmas cut-off dates and production times per country that are current in the desk and identical to what the website and the app show
Clean shift handover between Amsterdam, New York, Colombo and New Delhi so a WhatsApp conversation continues without repeating the story
Macros and help center articles in ten languages that match the current product rules: cover thresholds, extra-page prices, seven currencies, the Instagram withdrawal
Seeing that complaints they tag as a print defect or a curation miss actually reach production operations and the curation team
winsThem: A support desk that opens WhatsApp, e-mail and chat in one queue with the customer's orders, shipments and print files already attached
Reprint and refund handling that reroutes a reprint to the nearest partner with priority and shows the agent the new delivery estimate to quote
A Trustpilot and app store review inbox with a 48-hour countdown, the linked order and a suggested reply in the customer's language
Root-cause tags on every ticket that produce a weekly list the agent can hand to operations, the curation team and the growth team
Proactive delay notifications that answer the where-is-my-order question before the customer writes

Approving a reprint that ships to the same wrong address because the desk did not show the address change the customer made an hour earlier
A negative Trustpilot review passing the 48-hour mark unanswered during a peak weekend shift and being visible to the next 35,000 readers

jobsToBeDone.name: Resolve an order problem in one contact

jobsToBeDone.outcome: The customer leaves the conversation with the problem solved or a precise delivery statement, the ticket carries a resolution code and root-cause tag, and no colleague in the next time zone has to reopen it.

steps.step: Identify the customer and the order from the channel

Multi-book and gift orders often arrive under a different name than the recipient.

Changes after production starts are handled as a reprint or refund decision instead.

streamsNeeded.name: Resolve Support Requests And Reprints

streamsNeeded.name: Choose Format Price And Checkout

customerJourneyStories.name: A new night-shift agent in Colombo adopts the support desk
customerJourneyStories.summary: An agent who joins the outsourced support pod in Colombo to cover the US evening and night hours learns the PastBook support desk during the run-up to Q4, doubts whether she can decide reprints and refunds for American customers from Sri Lanka, and within one peak season handles where-is-my-order, address fixes and reprints in one contact.

stages.narrative: She joins the Colombo pod that covers the United States evening and night, PastBook's largest market with about 80% of customers, weeks before the Year in Review peak. Her previous employer handled telecom tickets from a spreadsheet and three separate tools; she has never worked orders that turn into physical books printed by partners on another continent.

In onboarding the team lead shows her the support desk that PastBook uses across the Netherlands, United States, Sri Lanka and India: WhatsApp, e-mail and chat in one queue, every contact opening with the customer's orders, print files and carrier tracking attached, and a shift-handover note from the Amsterdam morning. She reads the help center in English first and sees the same articles exist in ten languages.

She wonders whether she is allowed to decide a reprint for a customer in Texas at 2 a.m. Amsterdam time. What convinces her is that the desk encodes the policy: reprint and refund authority per agent level, the delivery windows per country and the Christmas cut-offs as data rather than memory, and the reprint button that shows where the job would be reprinted and when it would arrive.

Her first shifts are shadowed: she works tracking questions against the US 4–8 business day window, changes addresses before production starts, and approves her first reprint for a book with a colour cast, watching it route to the US partner as a priority job. A senior in New York reviews her closing notes and root-cause tags.

By the second half of the peak she handles a full queue: WhatsApp conversations that started in the New Delhi shift continue in hers without the customer repeating, she reprints and refunds within her authority, and she quotes delivery statements she trusts because the carrier data is in front of her. Her first-contact resolution climbs toward the pod average.

She stays with the pod after the peak because the desk made her decisions safe and visible: her reprint and refund calls were audited and upheld, her root-cause tags show up in the weekly list that operations acts on, and she is asked to write the Sinhala-speaking pod's first macro set for the Facebook import questions that cluster in her hours.

customerJourneyStories.name: A senior Amsterdam agent takes over the review and root-cause loop
customerJourneyStories.summary: A senior agent in Amsterdam who has answered tickets for three years is asked to own the Trustpilot and app store review inbox and the weekly root-cause report, resists doing it in spreadsheets, and adopts the desk's review inbox and tagging so complaints become partner audits and curation fixes.

stages.narrative: After a peak season in which several negative Trustpilot reviews were answered late because they lived in a separate browser tab, the support lead asks the most experienced Amsterdam agent to own the public review replies and the weekly complaint report to operations and product.

She learns that the desk can pull Trustpilot, App Store and Google Play reviews into the same queue as tickets, match them to orders and show a 48-hour countdown, and that root-cause tags on tickets can be aggregated per partner facility, country and cause without exporting anything. A colleague in the growth team shows her the reviews dashboard they already watch for ratings.

Her concern is that tagging costs the team time it does not have in Q4 and that nobody downstream will act. She evaluates a month of tags against the reprint cases and sees that two partner facilities and one curation issue explain most defects; production operations confirms they would audit a partner on that evidence. The company's public promise, replies to 100% of negative reviews typically within 48 hours, becomes measurable per shift.

For one quarter she runs the loop for real: every negative review answered from the inbox with the linked order, a mandatory root-cause tag before closing, and a weekly list to operations, the curation team and commerce. The first result is a partner corrective action on binding and a fix for a promo code that confused customers in Brazil.

The review inbox and the weekly root-cause report become part of the Amsterdam shift routine; agents in all four locations tag consistently because the taxonomy is in the desk, and the help center articles she updates deflect the questions she saw repeating.

She keeps ownership because the loop gives her leverage she never had on the front line: the one-star share stays around the 2% Trustpilot shows publicly while volume grows, the causes she reports are visibly closed by operations and the curation team, and she now trains new agents in Colombo and New Delhi on why a tag is worth ten seconds.

customerJourneyStories.name: A performance marketer moves the Year in Review campaign into the campaign console
customerJourneyStories.summary: A performance marketer hired in New York to grow the US market inherits a Q4 plan spread over ad platforms, spreadsheets and a promo list, is sceptical that an internal console can replace the ad managers she knows, and after one peak runs the Year in Review campaign across countries and currencies from the console with daily return on ad spend.

stages.narrative: She joins in August, weeks before the Year in Review campaign that produces the largest share of the year's orders, and finds last year's plan in ad platform exports, a promo spreadsheet in seven currencies and a Slack thread about cut-off dates. Nobody can tell her the real blended acquisition cost of last Q4 per country.

The CMO walks her through the growth and campaign console the Amsterdam team built: the seasonal calendar per country, promo codes created once and localised, attribution joined to installs and orders, and the funnel from install to permission to preview to order. The Milan colleague shows how the ten-language creatives are managed against one plan.

Her doubt is whether attribution in the console matches what the ad platforms claim and whether the console will slow her down in the peak. She evaluates a back-test on last Q4: the console's install-to-order and return-on-ad-spend numbers per country reconcile with finance, and it separates organic and featured installs that platforms were claiming. The promo cost view shows the discount share of revenue for the first time.

She runs the Mother's Day-scale September test in two countries from the console: campaigns, promo codes in USD and CAD, creatives in English and French, attribution read daily. When a Canadian code leaks to US customers, the console shows it the same day and she switches it off.

Q4 runs entirely from the console: cut-off dates per country feed the campaign end dates, budgets are rebalanced weekly between the US, Australia and the UK on return on ad spend, and the funnel view sends a curation slowdown to engineering before it shows up as wasted spend.

She keeps the console after the peak because it gave her the number she was hired for: a blended acquisition cost per country she can defend, a Q4 plan for next year that starts from data instead of exports, and a promo discipline the CMO now reviews weekly with her. She asks for the calendar and poster pushes to be planned there too.

customerJourneyStories.name: A CRM marketer builds the yearbook reminder programme
customerJourneyStories.summary: A lifecycle marketer in Amsterdam who ran generic newsletters is asked to make the annual yearbook a habit, questions whether reminders can be timed per customer and country without a large CRM suite, and adopts the console's lifecycle programmes to lift repeat orders while staying within consent rules.

stages.narrative: The management team sets a year-3 goal of an annual memory habit with a much higher repeat rate, and the CRM marketer realises the monthly newsletter she sends to everyone in English cannot deliver it: a family that ordered a yearbook in January and a grandparent who received a Christmas gift need different messages at different times.

In the growth and campaign console she finds lifecycle programmes that trigger from each customer's order history and country: yearbook reminders, calendar pushes in October, abandoned-preview recovery with the customer's own cover as the creative, rating prompts after delivery, and reorder and gift-copy flows. The support team tells her which reminders customers complain about.

She weighs it against buying a CRM suite. What decides it is that the console already has the order history, the consent records and the ten-language templates, that unsubscribes and GDPR and CCPA deletions propagate automatically, and that a yearbook reminder converting at a few percent of last year's customers pays for itself against paid acquisition at about USD 26 per customer.

Her first programme is the yearbook reminder for US customers who ordered in the previous year's first quarter, in English, with a control group. Conversion beats the newsletter several times over, and the console shows that reminders sent before the highlight video was shared perform worse, so she sequences them.

Within a year the lifecycle calendar covers the seven currencies and ten languages: yearbook and calendar reminders, reorders of earlier Facebook years for archivists, gift copies for grandparents before Christmas, and rating prompts that keep the App Store rating eligible for featuring. Repeat share becomes a weekly number in the growth meeting.

She stays on the console because repeat orders became her metric rather than open rates: customers ordering in two consecutive years rise, the programme runs without her touching send lists, and the growth and brand teams now ask her to add the sustainability and FSC story to the retention flow for European customers.

top.name: Blended customer acquisition cost
top.description: Total paid marketing spend divided by all new customers in the period, including organic, featured and referred customers, across all countries and currencies converted to USD. Modeled seed value for a US-heavy performance marketing mix; not an official PastBook figure.

customers.name: Production and Fulfilment Operations Manager
customers.description: Runs PastBook's production and fulfilment from Amsterdam or New York without owning a single press: books, calendars and posters are produced by partner printing facilities on four continents, most of them in the country of the customer, and shipped to 150+ countries. The manager owns the routing rules that send each paid order to the nearest facility with capacity and acceptable cost, the partner SLAs and integrations by API or hot folder, print specifications including FSC-certified paper and colour profiles, the delivery windows published per country (United States 4–8 business days after production, United Kingdom 4–5, France, the Netherlands, Italy and Germany 3–5, rest of the EU 5–7, Canada and Australia 5–10, New Zealand, India and Brazil 7–10), reprint root causes and the unit cost of a book against a small hardcover retail price of USD 19.99. The year is decided in the Q4 peak, when volume multiplies, Christmas cut-offs per country must hold, and every partner's capacity, quality and carrier performance is tested at once; production starts on payment, so there is no buffer to hide in.
careAbout: A production control tower that shows every paid order from print file to partner acceptance, production, carrier handover and delivery against the SLA and the published window for its country
Routing rules that put cost, capacity, product type and the customer's country together, and that can be changed in minutes when a partner falls behind in the peak
Print defect and reprint root causes per partner facility with the order and print file evidence, so audits and corrective actions rest on data rather than anecdotes
Capacity forecasts for Q4 agreed with marketing, contracted per region with a backup partner, and monitored daily against actual intake
Unit production and shipping cost per product and partner that make the gross margin behind a USD 19.99 small hardcover visible
Sustainability commitments that hold in production: FSC-certified paper, local printing to cut shipping emissions, made-to-order with no stock
winsThem: A control tower that monitors production SLA and quality per partner, flags stuck or rejected jobs and lets the manager reroute in one action
Routing that models the nearest facility, capacity, unit cost and product type per country, and switches to a backup automatically when a partner misses SLA
Partner integrations by order API or hot folder with status callbacks, so partner acceptance and production progress arrive without e-mails
Quality and reprint analytics that join support tickets, print files and partner batches into root causes per facility
Peak planning that turns the marketing forecast into contracted capacity per region and daily intake versus capacity dashboards
theirFear: A US partner missing its SLA in the second week of December with no contracted backup, so thousands of Year in Review books miss Christmas and become refunds
A colour profile or binding defect at one facility that is discovered from Trustpilot reviews weeks later instead of from a quality check at the partner
Unit cost creeping up through cross-border shipping and rerouting while retail prices and discounts stay where marketing set them

jobsToBeDone.outcome: Orders are produced and handed to carriers within SLA and arrive within the published delivery windows in every country, exceptions are caught and rerouted before the customer notices, and marketing and support quote windows that hold.

customerJourneyStories.name: A new operations manager runs the first holiday peak from the production control tower
customerJourneyStories.summary: An operations manager who joins from a photo company with its own factories has to run PastBook's partner network through Q4 without owning a press, distrusts a dashboard she did not build, and after one peak runs routing, capacity and cut-offs from the production control tower.

stages.narrative: She joins in September from a European photo products company that ran its own plants and finds that PastBook produces everything through partner facilities on four continents, that production starts on payment, and that the previous manager tracked partner status by e-mail and a weekly call. The Q4 peak is ten weeks away.

The print and fulfilment engineering team shows her the production control tower they built on the order feed: every paid order from print file to partner acceptance, production, carrier handover and delivery against the SLA and the published window per country, capacity ceilings per partner, and the reroute action. The customer support lead shows her how the same delivery windows appear in the desk.

Her worry is that partner status in the tower is only as good as the partner callbacks and that in a crisis she will still be on the phone. She evaluates it on last year's data: the tower would have shown the US partner's slippage four days before support saw the complaints, and the routing rules could have moved volume to the backup. She agrees to run the peak from it, with the phone as fallback.

In October she runs the first weeks of intake from the tower: capacity versus forecast per partner each morning, two reroutes when a preflight rule rejected files at the EU partner, and cut-off dates per country published to the website and support from the tower's production and window data.

In the peak weeks the tower is her day: intake against contracted capacity per region, overflow to the backup partner in the US before the primary hits its ceiling, gift orders reprioritised near cut-off, carrier lanes to Australia watched daily, and one message to support when a lane slipped instead of a flood of tickets.

She keeps the tower after the peak because it carried the year's decisive quarter: on-time production held above target, the backup contract paid for itself in one week, and the peak scorecard per partner is the basis of the contracts she renegotiates in January. She asks engineering to add the unit cost view so the same screen shows margin next to SLA.

customerJourneyStories.name: The quality lead adopts the control tower's reprint root-cause and partner audit workflow
customerJourneyStories.summary: A production quality lead in the operations team who tracked defects in a spreadsheet from support e-mails doubts that tickets, print files and partner batches can be joined automatically, adopts the control tower's quality monitoring and audit workflow, and turns reprint causes into partner corrective actions and preflight rules.

stages.narrative: After a quarter in which a binding defect at one facility showed up first in Trustpilot reviews and then in reprint costs, the quality lead is asked to make defects visible before customers see them. His spreadsheet of support e-mails cannot say which partner batch or which print file the complaints belong to.

He sees that the control tower's quality monitoring joins the support desk's root-cause tags and photos with the partner batch, the print file and the preflight report, and that audits and corrective actions per partner facility can be scheduled and tracked there. The support team's weekly root-cause list already arrives in that format.

He questions whether the partners will accept findings derived from customer photos. Testing it on one facility, the joined view shows a colour profile issue on one product only, the partner confirms it from its own quality check log, and the fix takes days rather than a quarter. The tower's defect definitions match the print specification every partner signed.

For one quarter he runs the loop from the tower for two facilities: weekly root-cause review with support, audit findings and corrective actions recorded per partner, and two new preflight rules that stop the file errors the EU partner kept rejecting.

Quality monitoring becomes the operations rhythm: defects caught at partner quality checks rise, reprint causes per facility are reviewed with each partner monthly, FSC paper compliance is tracked per batch, and the sustainability team uses the same data for the local-production and paper claims on the website.

He stays with the workflow because it changed his relationship with partners from complaints to shared evidence: corrective actions close within weeks, the same defect no longer recurs after a fix, and the peak review now includes a quality scorecard per facility that decides which partners get volume next year.

top.name: On-time production and shipping rate
top.description: Share of paid orders that are produced by the routed partner facility and handed to the carrier within the partner SLA, across all products and countries. Modeled seed value for a partner network on four continents; not an official PastBook figure.

branches.name: Production and delivery speed
branches.description: How fast paid orders enter production, leave the partner facility and reach the customer against the SLA and the published delivery windows.

children.name: Production within SLA rate
children.description: Share of jobs produced within the partner's contracted production time, from acceptance to ready for carrier pickup.

children.name: Median hours from payment to production start
children.description: Median hours between payment and the partner confirming production start; production starts on payment, so rendering, preflight and partner acceptance are the only steps in between.

children.name: Q4 peak on-time production rate
children.description: Share of jobs produced within SLA during the October to December peak weeks.

children.name: Delivered within published delivery window
children.description: Share of parcels delivered within the window published for the destination country after production (US 4–8 business days, UK 4–5, FR/NL/IT/DE 3–5, EU 5–7, CA/AU 5–10, NZ/IN/BR 7–10).

children.name: Carrier on-time rate United States
children.description: Share of US parcels delivered within 4–8 business days after production, the largest market.

children.name: Carrier on-time rate Europe and United Kingdom
children.description: Share of parcels to the UK (4–5 business days), FR/NL/IT/DE (3–5) and the rest of the EU (5–7) delivered within their windows.

branches.name: Print quality and rework
branches.description: Whether books leave every facility to the same specification and how quickly the causes of defects are found and closed.

children.name: Print defect rate
children.description: Share of produced orders with a print, binding, colour or cropping defect, whether caught at the partner's quality check or reported by the customer; drives the customer-facing reprint rate of about 1.6% together with transit loss and address errors.

children.name: Defects caught at partner quality check before shipping
children.description: Share of print defects found and remade at the partner before the parcel ships.

children.name: Reprints caused by print defects per 1,000 orders
children.description: Customer-facing reprints attributed to a print defect per thousand orders; the defects that escaped the partner check.

children.name: Reprint root causes closed within 30 days
children.description: Share of identified reprint root causes, per partner facility or file issue, with a corrective action verified within 30 days.

children.name: Partner quality audits completed per quarter
children.description: Number of partner facility audits, on site or remote sample checks, completed per quarter across the network.

children.name: Colour and binding complaints per 1,000 orders
children.description: Customer complaints about colour or binding per thousand orders, the two most frequent defect types.

top.name: Unit fulfilment cost per order
top.description: Average partner production cost, packaging, shipping, reprint allowance and partner management overhead per paid order in USD, against an average order value of about USD 36.50. Modeled seed value; not an official PastBook figure.

branches.name: Production and shipping cost
branches.description: What the partner charges per book and what it costs to get the parcel to the customer, by product and country.

children.name: Unit production cost per book
children.description: Average partner production cost per book across small and large hardcovers and the page mix; a small hardcover retails at USD 19.99 for 24 pages plus USD 0.40 per extra page.

children.name: Paper and print cost per page
children.description: Partner cost per printed page including FSC-certified paper, against an extra-page retail price of USD 0.40 (small) and USD 0.55 (large).

children.name: FSC-certified paper share of production
children.description: Share of produced books, calendars and posters printed on FSC-certified paper across all partner facilities.

children.name: Shipping cost per order
children.description: Average carrier cost per order across countries and service levels, including cross-border shipments when no local partner is available.

children.name: Orders shipped domestically from a local partner
children.description: Share of orders produced in the destination country, which cuts shipping cost and emissions.

children.name: Multi-product orders consolidated in one parcel
children.description: Share of orders with several products shipped as one parcel on the longest production time rather than split.

branches.name: Partner network resilience and margin
branches.description: Whether every region has redundant capacity for the peak and how much gross margin an order leaves after fulfilment.

children.name: Regions with redundant partner capacity
children.description: Share of shipping regions (US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India, Brazil) with a contracted backup facility able to take peak overflow.

children.name: Active partner facilities
children.description: Number of partner printing facilities with a live integration and volume in the last quarter, across four continents.

children.name: Peak capacity utilisation
children.description: Peak-week production volume as a share of contracted network capacity; above about 90% quality and SLA start to break.

children.name: Gross margin per order after fulfilment
children.description: Average order value of about USD 36.50 minus unit fulfilment cost per order, before marketing and payment fees.

children.name: Average order value
children.description: Average paid order value in USD across books, calendars, posters and gift cards after discounts.

children.name: Reprint and refund cost per order
children.description: Failure recovery cost per order: reprint production and shipping plus refunded revenue; about USD 47 per hundred orders today.

productStrategy.vision: Run PastBook's partner printing network on four continents as one production system: routing, SLAs, capacity, quality and unit cost visible in a single control tower, most orders produced in the customer's country on FSC-certified paper, redundant capacity in every region for the holiday peak, and reprint root causes closed at the partner or in the preflight rules, so books arrive within the published windows at a cost that keeps margin under a USD 19.99 entry price.

year1.focus: Stabilise peak-season SLAs across partners: put every paid order in the production control tower from print file to delivery, make routing capacity-aware with a tested backup in the US and the EU, and bring reprint root causes, print defects and unit cost per partner into one view before the next Q4.
